memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: but the judge must not impose more than forty lashes. If the guilty party is flogged more than that, your fellow Israelite will be degraded in your eyes. - Deut 25:3 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
God set a firm limit on punishment, no more than forty lashes. Why? So that the guilty person would not be "degraded in your eyes." Even someone being punished for wrongdoing was still a fellow human being, still made in God's image, and was not to be humiliated or treated as less than human. God placed a boundary on justice to protect human dignity.

This is remarkable. Even in the context of deserved punishment, God cared about the dignity of the offender. The wrongdoer was still a brother, not to be brutalised or shamed beyond measure. God's justice never strips people of their fundamental worth. There is a restraint here rooted in the value of every person.

This teaches us something important about how we treat others, even when they are in the wrong. It is easy to feel that someone who has done wrong deserves whatever they get, to pile on shame and contempt. But God calls us to remember the dignity of every person, even those we must correct or hold accountable. We can address wrongdoing without dehumanising the wrongdoer. This reflects the heart of Christ, who upheld both truth and mercy, never crushing the broken. When you must confront or correct someone, do you still honour their God-given dignity, or are you tempted to degrade them?

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Do you honour the dignity of those you must correct?
2. Where are you tempted to pile on shame or contempt?
3. How can you hold truth and mercy together like Christ?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Lord, help me address wrong without degrading the wrongdoer. Give me Your heart that upholds both truth and the dignity of every person. Amen.
